author: Bibi
name_in_asr: Mungali (Mung-kie-li)
asr_identification: Mingora (Tucci) or Manglawar (Deane), Swat district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; undecided
evidence: Reports Cunningham (Mangora of Mogal Beg, Manglora of Court's map), Deane 1896 ('undoubtedly Minglaur (Manglawar) and not Mingaur'), and Tucci 1958 (Mingora, not Manglawar). No evidence of her own.
quote: H.A. Deane (1896: 656) wrote that Mungali is undoubtedly Minglaur (Manglawar) and not Mingaur (Mingora). But G. Tucci (1958: 288) strongly believed that Mungali or Ming chie li can be identified as Mingora and not with Manglawar.
note: Agrees with the study that the question is open (Mingora, Mizutani and the Italian mission; Manglaor the rival); adds Deane's explicit rejection of Mingora and Tucci's explicit choice. Does not decide.

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: great stupa 4 or 5 li to the east of Mungali (Rishi of Peace / Kṣāntivādin)
asr_identification: Butkara I, Mingora, Swat, Pakistan (Tucci 1958)
evidence: Tucci (1958, p. 288) identified the stūpa with Butkara I, which he also took for Songyun's Ta-lo monastery with its gilded images; the Italian mission's excavation at Butkara I found sculpture with traces of gold wash.
quote: Xuanzang further elaborates that 4 or 5 li to the east of Mungali is a great stupa, where the Buddha had lived as the ‘Rishi of Peace’ and sacrificed his body organs for Kali-raja in one of his previous births. Tucci (1958: 288) identified this site with Butkara-I.
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (unlocated): Tucci's Butkara I is a candidate the study does not list. It depends on Mingora as the capital (03.01.01a); the gilding evidence bears on Songyun's monastery, not on the Kṣāntivādin legend.

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: foot print of the Buddha (Tirath); rock for washing the Buddha's clothes
asr_identification: Tirat (Madyan, Jinki Khel), upper Swat; the footprint stone now in the Swat Museum; the clothes-washing rock on the right bank of the Swat, since blasted
evidence: The footprint stone with its Kharoṣṭhī inscription (Bühler; Konow, CII II) is now displayed in the Swat Museum; Stein saw a large mound of a demolished stūpa by it, with a local tradition of a 'Gumbat', no longer visible; Tucci found Buddhist sculpture in situ around. The washing rock Stein found on the right bank, with Sanskrit and Arabic graffiti, 'has been blasted some years back' (R. Khan 2014).
quote: Stein (1972: 86) identified this place with the village of Tirath (Madyan, Jinki khel) in the Upper Swat, and the foot prints bearing Kharoshthi inscription are now on display in the Swat Museum…It is said that this rock has been blasted some years back (Khan 2014: 96-97).
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Tirat; the rock on the road towards Tirat, Stein). Adds the present state: the footprint stone moved to the Swat Museum, the washing rock destroyed (per Khan 2014), so the point for 03.01.04a can no longer be checked on the ground.

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: Mo-su Sangharama; Stupa of Dove-ransoming (Sivi jātaka)
asr_identification: Gumbatai stūpa, Torwasak village (Mo-su) and the Girarai ruins (Śibi stūpa), Buner, Pakistan (Stein, via Rienjang 2012); Deane: Chanai hills at Surkhavi and the Naranji valley ruins for the Śibi stūpa
evidence: Stein's identifications as summarised by Rienjang 2012: Mo-su = the Gumbatai stūpa of Torwasak; Śibi stūpa = the Girarai ruins. Deane had put the Śibi stūpa at the Chanai hills (Surkhavi) or the Naranji valley, but found no stūpa there, only Gandharan sculpture fragments.
quote: These two stupas are identified by Stein as Gumbatai stupa of Torwasak village and Girarai ruins respectively (Rienjang 2012 :4). The ruins on Chanai hills located in the Surkhavi village and the Naranji valley ruins have been identified by Deane as the place of the stupa built by Ashoka to the west of Mo-su monastery
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani: 03.01.07 Gogdara (Mizuno) or Sura (Cunningham); 03.01.08 unlocated. Stein's Torwasak (Gumbatai) and Girarai and Deane's Surkhavi/Naranji are candidates the study does not list; they follow from Stein's Panjkotai for Mahāvana (03.01.06), which the study accepts, so they are worth checking in Stein's own report (Bibi gives only Rienjang's summary).

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: valley of Shan-ni lo-shi; convent of Sa-pao-sha-ti and its 80-ft stupa
asr_identification: Adinzai valley, Lower Dir (Deane); Andan Dheri and Sapar (Saparuna) as the sites of the monuments (R. Khan 2014)
evidence: Deane's Adinzai valley; R. Khan (2014, p. 106) names Andan Dheri and Sapar (Saparuna) as the probable sites of the monastery and stūpa. No evidence given.
quote: Andan-dheri and Sapar (Saparuna) are believed to be the probable sites for these sacred monuments (Khan 2014: 106).
note: Agrees with the study on the valley (Adinzai, Deane); for the stūpa it adds Andan Dheri and Sapar beside the study's Suma stūpa (Deane). The claim is Khan's, unargued here.

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: Ho-pu-to-shi (miraculous stone) stupa; vihara with an image of Avalokiteshvara
asr_identification: the natural stone niche at Shahkhorai village, Swat (Tucci); a rock-carved Buddha with ruins of a small vihāra and a stūpa base nearby (Tucci 1958)
evidence: Tucci took the huge dome-shaped natural stone niche at Shahkhorai, beside a large rock image of the Buddha and minor carvings, for the miraculous stone stūpa; for the Avalokiteśvara vihāra, 30–40 li W across the river, he noted a rock-carved Buddha with ruins of a small vihāra and a stūpa base in the vicinity (Tucci 1958, pp. 305–306).
quote: Tucci opines that this miraculous stupa is situated at the village of Shahkhorai, which was a very holy place because of the presence of the huge rock image of the Buddha and other minor carvings in the nearby rocks…Tucci (1958: 305-306) has also mentioned an image of the Buddha carved in a rock with ruins of a small vihara and the base of a stupa in the same vicinity.
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (both unlocated; Deane's extant stūpa doubted by Watters): Tucci's Shahkhorai is a candidate the study does not list, resting on a natural rock read as the 'stone stūpa'. Its bearing and distance from the capital are not tested. The vihāra candidate is not named precisely.

author: Bibi
name_in_asr: Ta-li-lo valley; wooden Maitreya
asr_identification: Darel valley, right bank of the Indus (Tucci 1977); the gold ornament from Pattan (Indus Kohistan) linked to the image
evidence: A gold necklace/girdle of c. 16 kg found by a shepherdess at Pattan, Indus Kohistan (once in the Peshawar Museum, now at the State Bank of Pakistan), was attributed by Farooq Swati and Nasim Khan (Khan 1997–98) to the lost wooden Maitreya, taken as archaeological proof of the image in Indus Kohistan.
quote: Scholars like Farooq Swati and Nasim Khan are of the opinion that this heavy gold ornament most probably belonged to this wooden figure of Bodhisattva Maitreya which has perished long before…The archaeological evidence of this gold neck girdle thus attests the presence of this colossal wooden image of Maitreya in the locale of the Indus Kohistan (Khan 1997-98: 127-138).
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani on Darel. The Pattan ornament is a conjectural link (Pattan lies in Kohistan, downstream of Darel, not in it) and is not site evidence; Hameed 2015 calls it a Scythian girdle.

author: Dar & Hameed
name_in_asr: Singhapura (capital city)
asr_identification: Sheranwali Khanqah (now Sheranwala Nakka / Sangi), twin round mounds at Nakka Jaba, c. 5 km N of Katas Raj and E of Dulmial, Chakwal district, Punjab, Pakistan
evidence: Field visits 1994 and April 2019: two circular, domed mounds, each with a large jand tree and Muslim graves (a headless crouching stone lion on the main grave in 1994, since looted by tunnelling), strewn with plain red-slipped polished pottery; a pond beside the smaller mound; the Katas temples are visible from the top. Katas lies due S and Murti SE of the spot, as the text has the two Aśoka stūpas. The names Sheranwali ('of the lions') and Sangi are read as echoes of Siṃha(pura) and saṅgha. Not excavated; the authors call the tree argument provisional and say they are 'tempted to relate to, if not to identify' the site.
quote: The old site (Pls.XVII) is exactly east of Dulmial and north of Katas at a distance of some 5 kilometers from the latter…Thus, keeping in view the above points, we are justifiedin identifying the sites of Sheranwali Khanqah, the Katas Raj and the Murti as the sites of the city of Singhapura and the two sacred sites
note: Differs in site, not in direction, from the study (Stein's field of ruins 1–2 miles N of Ketas; rival Malot) and from Mizutani (Kotera fort above Ketas). The candidate is unexcavated and rests on two mounds, surface pottery and the place-name; the circuit (14–15 li) is not tested. An alternative to record; no site evidence.

author: Dar & Hameed
name_in_asr: Singhapura (capital city)
asr_identification: not Dulmial (Stein) nor Malot (Cunningham), Chakwal district, Pakistan
evidence: Dulmial, 3 miles NW of Katas, was proposed by Stein from earlier (Greek and Indo-Scythian) coins bought at Katas and said to come from Dulmial; on a visit in April 2019 the authors found no ancient mound in or near the town, and the local museum owner knew of no antiquities from it; Stein apparently never went there. Malot has no stūpa or temple by a sacred pool to its S or SE, and its temple is later than Xuanzang.
quote: It was ashock to learn and see that there is no ancient mound with in the present town of Dulmial or within its immediate vicinity…Once it was a strong candidate for the site of Singhapura, but it is no more considered so simply for the reason that we do not see any stupa or a hindu temple by the side of a sacred pool further south or south-east of it
note: Bears on the study's alternatives: the Jhelum gazetteer's Stein text, as the study quotes it, puts the town on 'the field of ruins lying one or two miles further north' of Ketas; Dar & Hameed quote a different Stein passage naming Dulmial, 3 miles NW. If Stein meant Dulmial, the 2019 visit removes the site evidence for it. Also weakens the Malot alternative (Cunningham ASR II, V). Mizutani's Kotera is set aside implicitly (Stein rejected it).

author: Dar & Hameed
name_in_asr: stupa built by Asoka-raja, south of the capital (Katas)
asr_identification: the square stūpa base at Katas Raj, before the Sat-Ghara temples, Chakwal district, Pakistan
evidence: The square stūpa basement at Katas (Cunningham's plan, ASR II p. 190, where it was 'mistaken as Temple') was excavated and partly restored in 2011 (pls. V–VIII); the authors take it as the earliest building on the site, Buddhist in origin, later used by Jainas and Hindus; Cunningham saw remains of monasteries on the hill of the present Youth Hostel. It lies due S of their capital.
quote: The earliest site that can still be seen on this site is the extensive base of square stupa which was visited by Hiuen Tsang in 631 but it was claimed to have been built long before his visit by the Emperor Asoka…Plans of Buddhist/Jaian Stupa (right) mistaken as Temple
note: Agrees with the study (the large stūpa before the E front of the Sat-Ghara temples, Stein) and with Mizutani's base at the foot of the Kotera hill; adds the 2011 excavation of the base, which settles Cunningham's 'temple' reading in favour of a stūpa. The study's open question whether the sources describe one structure is answered: it is the same basement (Cunningham's plan).

author: Dar & Hameed
name_in_asr: second stupa with ten tanks, SE of the capital; sacred spot of the White-robed; deva temple (Murti)
asr_identification: Murti, Rakh Gandala (Gandhala valley), near Choa Saidan Shah, Chakwal district, Pakistan
evidence: Murti lies SE of Sheranwali Khanqah and c. 3 miles E of Katas; Stein (1889, 1930–31) excavated a stūpa (in its last phase probably Jaina) and a Hindu temple E and N of it, whose sculpture, all of Murti red sandstone, went to the Lahore Museum; Stein saw several pools of clear water with fish in the Ghatia/Ghata nala; site under the ASI protection board of 1929, seen in 1994; the former stūpa site seen in April 2019.
quote: As Aurel Stein's two visits of this site n 1889 and 1930 has proven beyond doubt, there stood here in 631 ACE and in later periods, a Buddhist/Jaina Stupa, a Hindu Temple…in 1930, Sir Aurel Stein saw this nullah taking the shape of several pools of pure water with numerous fish in them
note: Agrees with the study (Murti, Stein) for both the stone stūpa with pools (03.04.03) and the Jaina site (03.04.x1); differs from Mizutani (Ketas pools). Adds the 2019 condition of the site; no new excavation. The 40–50 li SE is not measured from their capital (c. 3 miles from Katas to Murti).

author: Filigenzi
name_in_asr: Uttarasena stūpa of the Chinese sources
asr_identification: Shingardar (Shankardar) stūpa near Ghalegai (Deane, Stein) or Nawe-kalai (Barabru), lat. 34°39'N, long. 72°11'E (Tucci), Swat, Pakistan
evidence: Tucci (1958, pp. 294, 299–302) rejected Deane's and Stein's Shingardar as highly unlikely and put the Uttarasena stūpa at Nawe-kalai, where excavation in the late 1980s found a Buddhist sacred area (Abdul Nasir and Faiz-ur-Rehman 1996, 'Barabru'), with rock reliefs C120–C122 and traces of ancient canals nearby. At Ghalegai, Stein's reading of relief C116 in the Hindu-ghar cave as Uttarasena the donor is rejected by Filigenzi on dating (late, comparable with Palola Ṣāhi bronzes). Filigenzi does not decide between the stūpas.
quote: A short distance away lies the Shingardar stūpa, which Deane and Stein, but not Tucci, identified as the Uttarasena stūpa of the Chinese sources…The locality, which Tucci identified as the site of the Uttarasena stūpa, was excavated in the late 1980s; a Buddhist sacred area was discovered.
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Shankardar stūpa, E bank of the Swat; medium): Tucci's Nawe-kalai is a rival the study does not list, now with an excavated Buddhist sacred area. Nawe-kalai at 72°11'E lies W of Barikot, and the text has the stūpa 60–70 li SW of the capital on the E bank of the river; the bearing is not tested here. Record as an open alternative; Tucci's argument (1958, pp. 299–302) should be read.

author: Filigenzi
name_in_asr: Mengjieli; Mangala[p]or / Manglaor
asr_identification: Mingora ('formerly Mengjieli', after Olivieri 1996) for Xuanzang's capital; the Manglaor area = Mangala[p]or of the Tibetan sources (Tucci), Swat, Pakistan
evidence: Catalogue of rock sculptures by site: Mingora is labelled 'formerly Mengjieli' (citing Olivieri 1996, p. 71), with reliefs on the cliff above the NE sector of the Mingora bazaar along an old path to the Manglawar area over the Shamelai chain. The Manglaor area (four valleys) is the Mangala[p]or of the Tibetan sources (Tucci 1958, 1971); O rgyan pa mentions a temple founded by Indrabhūti called Mangalaor; Stein reported the Rasho-dherai stūpa ENE of Manglaor village.
quote: A first group of monuments is situated on the outskirts of the heavily urbanised area of Mingora (formerly Mengjieli; see Olivieri 1996: 71)…The area denoted by this name (the ancient Mangala[p]or of the Tibetan sources; see Tucci 1958: 286
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Mingora) as the Italian mission's working identification, but gives no argument (only a reference to Olivieri 1996); the Tibetan Mangala(p)ur = Manglaor link remains the basis of the rival. Does not settle the question; the place stays open.

author: Filigenzi
name_in_asr: stone statue of Bhīmā Devī; sanctuary of Maheśvara and Bhīmā
asr_identification: Mount Karamar (Cunningham, Foucher) or Kashmir Smast (Nasim Khan 2006), Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
evidence: Karamar: Cunningham's identification, which Foucher (1902, pp. 363–365) supported with a ziyārat on the hill, local Muslim veneration, a story of a fakir's leap from the summit, and the woman fakir Shehr Banu (= Siṃhavāhinī, an epithet of Durgā). Kashmir Smast: Nasim Khan (2006, pp. 11–13, 43) identifies Xuanzang's place there; Peshawar University surveys and small excavations found a Śaiva cult, and the name Bhīmā occurs widely in the inscriptions from the site (Falk 2003a; Nasim Khan 2006, pp. 74, 102–103; Srinivasan 2011). Filigenzi does not decide. She gives the image as c. 50 li NW of Po-lu-sha.
quote: In Mount Karamar, as we have seen, A. Foucher identifies a spot mentioned by Xuanzang. A different interpretation is given by Nasim Khan, who thinks that the place described by Xuanzang is to be identified with the site of Kashmir Smast (Nasim Khan 2006: 11-13, 43).…The name of Bhīmā is largely present among the epigraphic records from the site
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Karamar, Cunningham, no shrine found): Kashmir Smast has inscriptions naming Bhīmā and an excavated Śaiva cult, which is site evidence of the kind the study's confidence rule asks for, if the distance and bearing from Varuṣapura (text 50 li NE; Filigenzi's NW follows a translation) can be squared. Foucher's local-cult evidence for Karamar is new to the study. Record both; the Kashmir Smast reports (Nasim Khan 2006, Falk 2003) should be checked.

author: Kimmet
name_in_asr: Udabhāṇḍapura (U-to-kia-han-ch'a)
asr_identification: Hund, right (N) bank of the Indus, c. 25 km E of the Kabul–Indus confluence, Swabi district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
evidence: A late 10th-c. stone slab said to come from Hund bears a Śāradā inscription naming the town of Udabhāṇḍa north of the Indus under Jayapāladeva (r. c. 964–1002) (Rehman 1978, 1979; Agrawal 1985; Hargreaves 1926). Hargreaves (1926) saw the old fortification wall, scattered structures, a 12-ft semicircular foundation (stūpa or temple base) and two mounds NW of the village. Excavations by Ihsan Ali (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Directorate and Peshawar University, late 1990s–2000s) found Hindu Śāhi structures, unpublished as of 2012; Buddhist clay votive tablets and miniature stūpas; Śāhi coins without context; part of the site lost to the Indus. Kimmet concludes that contemporaneous archaeological evidence remains scant.
quote: Evidence of the Hindu Śāhi political center is found on a late 10th-century stone slab said to come from Hund that bears a śāradā inscription identifying the town of Udabhāṇḍa north of the Indus ruled by Jayapāladeva (r. c. 964-1002 CE)
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Hund). Adds an inscription said to come from Hund that names Udabhāṇḍa, against the study's 'No record is said to name the town' (the study cites only the Kāmeśvarīdevī slab and Hargreaves' Śaiva inscription); its provenance is reported ('said to come from'), so it is near-site evidence. Also records that the 1990s–2000s excavations remain unpublished.

author: Kuwayama
name_in_asr: カニシカ大塔 (Shah-ji-ki Dheri 主塔)
asr_identification: Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, E/SE of Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
evidence: Japanese original of the Shah-ji-ki-Dheri study (cf. Kuwayama 2002, ch. V): circular stūpa with radial walls, then square, then cruciform (the cruciform remodelling put after the 560s, in a Kashmir-influenced building phase). New beyond the 2002 summary in the study: an appendix lists every Chinese account of the Kaniṣka stūpa (Faxian, Daorong, Songyun, Weishu, Xiyu ji, Life, Xu gaoseng zhuan, Shijia fangzhi, Fayuan zhulin, Huichao) with their dimensions; Xuanzang's description (two small stūpas and two seated Buddhas 'under the bodhi tree' carved in blue-black stone on the S of the E stair; a 16-chi double-bodied Buddha; a white stone Buddha 100 paces SW; hundreds of small stūpas round it; the stūpa burnt and under repair when he arrived) points to Gandhāran schist sculpture, which the excavation hardly produced, and so argues against a cruciform stūpa in 629; the larger base circuit (1.5 li) in Xuanzang might reflect it, so the question is left open.
quote: しかしこれを大層西域記にみえるストゥ‑パまわりの彫刻とあわせてかんがえると,十字形ストゥ‑パとは考えがたくなる｡…Shah‑ji‑kiDheriの蓉掘ではこういった片岩やストゥッコの彫刻類はほとんど出土せず
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Shah-ji-ki-Dheri); bears on what Xuanzang saw, not on where. More detailed than the study's Kuwayama 2002 summary on one point: Xuanzang's own observations are read against the excavated phases (probably not yet cruciform in 629; under repair after a fire). No change to the location.

author: Kuwayama
name_in_asr: Shah-ji-ki Dheri (wheel-shaped foundation)
asr_identification: (structure only)
evidence: On the origin of the wheel-shaped (radial-wall) foundations of great stūpas (Amaravati and other Andhra stūpas, Sanghol, Dharmarājikā, Sirkap block 1E', Shah-ji-ki-Dheri), traced to the mausoleum of Augustus; Xuanzang is cited only for the 'northern border' character of the NW. Locates no Xiyu ji place.
note: No bearing on 02.04.03 (Shah-ji-ki-Dheri) or other identifications.

author: Miyaji
name_in_asr: 達麗羅 (Darel); 陀歴 (Faxian)
asr_identification: Darel valley, above the Indus, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan (assumed)
evidence: Textual: the image is attested by Faxian (wooden, 8 zhang, with an 8-chi base), Baoyun (gilded, 8 zhang, in the 名僧伝) and Fasheng (ox-head sandalwood, 8 xun, seen 'NE of Udyāna', 名僧伝), and Xuanzang (wooden, 100+ chi, 'in a great monastery in the Darel valley'). Miyaji, following Kuwayama 1987, notes that Xuanzang's route and his condensed retelling of Faxian's legend suggest he may not have seen the image himself. The identification 陀歴 = Darel is taken as given.
quote: 陀歴は現在のダレルに同定され,パミールとカラコルムの支脈を背にし,インダス河を眼下に見下す峡谷にある。…玄奘は,その行程と記述の仕方,法顕の伝承を簡略化したような書き方などからみて,ダレルの弥勒大仏を直接に見ていない可能性もある。
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Darel); no new site evidence. Adds Fasheng's bearing (NE of Udyāna), which fits a valley on the Indus NE of Swat, and supports the study's note that Xuanzang reports Darel by hearsay.

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: チャナカ・デリー遺跡 (Foucher's 'Kanaka-caitya', Songyun's 白象宮)
asr_identification: not Chanaka Dheri, c. 2 km NNE of Shahbaz Garhi, Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan: a palace, not a monastery
evidence: Re-reading of the unpublished Kyoto University excavations (Mizuno, 1959–67, six seasons) of the central and NW mounds: no stūpa and no Buddhist sculpture (one small fragment of a garland-bearer relief only); the lower level has two massive buildings (N court 72 × 47 m, with a hall of six pillars and a large water tank), taken as a palace built in the 1st c. AD (Indo-Parthian or early Kushan) and destroyed by an earthquake c. AD 200 under Vasudeva I; above it, village houses (Ranigat pottery periods 5–6, to the mid-6th c., with a Kidarite gold coin hoard; and again after the 9th c.). Cunningham had dug there for three days in 1871 and given up. Foucher (1901, 1915) took the site for Songyun's White Elephant monastery N of Varṣapura without excavating.
quote: しかし，発掘調査が進むに従って，チャナカ・デリー遺跡には仏教寺院の痕跡が残されていないことが明らかになった。仏教寺院遺跡に存在するはずのストゥーパの痕跡が，この遺跡では確認されなかったのである。…結局，チャナカ・デリー遺跡からはストゥーパなどの遺構も仏教彫刻などの遺物も発見されなかった。よって，同遺跡を仏教寺院遺跡と考えることはできない。
note: Agrees with the study (Chanaka Dheri shown by excavation to be a palace; the stūpa N of Varṣapura unlocated) and with Mizutani's report; adds the dated sequence (palace 1st c.–c. 200, village to the 6th c. and after the 9th) from the pottery, so the hill was a village, not a monastery, in Xuanzang's time. Naiki repeats Cunningham's Shahbaz Garhi = Varṣapura (02.04.14) without new evidence.

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: 宝蔵塔 (stūpa of the Four Great Treasures)
asr_identification: Dharmarājikā great stūpa (Chir Tope), Tamra Nala valley, Taxila, Rawalpindi district, Punjab, Pakistan
evidence: The Dharmarājikā stūpa (drum 34.5 m) is the largest in the area (Baoti Pind 19.5 m, 'Kunāla' base 19 × 31.5 m, Bhallar 13 m; table 1), so Xuanzang should have recorded it. Court J of the monastery (excavated 1930–31) held six skeletons of murdered people, one beheaded, crushed under the burnt collapse; among its 25 coins three are Hephthalite, one an Alkhan coin of Javukha, a king of c. 492/3, so the massacre is later than the late 5th century (probably after the mid-6th) and the bodies were never buried nor the monastery rebuilt: the site was deserted when Xuanzang came, as the text says of the Treasure stūpa's monastery (久絕僧徒). It lies between the Margala hills and the Hathial/Sarda hills ('between two mountains'). The stūpa of the Sacrificed Head still had monks, and the Kunāla stūpa would need a 7th-c. city NW of the Dharmarājikā, where Sirkap and Kachcha Kot are 2nd c. BC–2nd c. AD, so only the Treasure stūpa fits.
quote: 5 世紀末以降のある時期に発生した襲撃をもって，ダルマラージカーは活動を停止したと判断できる。7 世紀前葉に玄奘がタキシラを訪れた際には，寺院は荒廃し，無人であったと考えられる。…伽藍が荒廃し，すでに僧徒が住んでいないという記録は，まさにダルマラージカーの襲撃後の状況を表すかのようである。
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (the stūpa on the NE peak of the Baoti ridge above Baoti Pind, after Cunningham and Marshall). Naiki accepts Baoti Pind's distance as tolerable but argues from the size and the abandonment of the Dharmarājikā; a hypothesis, which also moves the capital (03.03.01a) 40+ li SE. If accepted it would resolve the study's E-for-SE bearing problem differently, measuring from a Rawalpindi capital.

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: タキシラの都城 (呾叉始羅國大都城)
asr_identification: central Rawalpindi, on the Pothohar plateau, Punjab, Pakistan (not Sirsukh)
evidence: If the Dharmarājikā is the Treasure stūpa, the city lay 40+ li (c. 17 km+) SE of it; central Rawalpindi lies 25 km SE. Cunningham (ASR II, pp. 151–152) recorded coins found yearly and ground covered with potsherds at the cantonment, Idgah, Sadar and the old bazaar, i.e. the city stands on a site. Sirsukh (2nd c. or later) was only cut at its S wall by Marshall, so its 7th-c. occupation is unproven (Kuwayama 1987). A Kharoṣṭhī copper plate naming Takhaśila (year 78 of Maues, 1st c. BC) is said to come from Hasan Abdal, 15 km NW of the Taxila valleys, so the name need not be tied to them. Survey of Islamabad (Rawal Dam mound, 1st–8th c. pottery; Ban Faqiran stūpa, 2nd c., on the old path across the Margala hills, excavated 2015–16) shows the plateau was occupied. Naiki calls this a hypothesis that needs excavation in Rawalpindi.
quote: ここで筆者は，玄奘の記録したタキシラの都城が現在のラーワルピンディー市中心部のどこかにあり，宝蔵塔がタムラー・ナーラー渓谷のダルマラージカー大塔に，捨頭塔がラーワルピンディー市中心部の北西 8km にあったトープに，拘浪拏塔が市中心部の南東 3.5km にあったトープに，それぞれ対応するという仮説を提示したい。
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Sirsukh, after Marshall; medium). Naiki uses the same gap the study's note records (no evidence of 7th-c. occupation of Sirsukh; Kuwayama) but offers no site evidence for Rawalpindi beyond Cunningham's surface finds; an alternative to record, not a replacement. It moves the whole Taxila frame (03.03.03, 03.03.04, 03.03.06) to the plateau; 03.03 as a country is not affected.

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: 捨頭塔 (stūpa of the Sacrificed Head)
asr_identification: the tope 5 miles NW of Rawalpindi, N of the road (Court 1836; Cunningham), now within Islamabad, Pakistan
evidence: Court's map (1836) marks two topes beside Rawalpindi; Cunningham (ASR II, pp. 151–152) visited them: one 5 miles NW of the city, N of the road, a long mound 20 ft high covered with stone fragments, where an old excavation had found the walls of a square temple, gone by his time. 12–13 li (c. 5 km) N of a Rawalpindi capital. Naiki adds that the name Margala ('cut neck') matches the meaning of Takṣaśilā and the head-gift legend. Naiki had not yet visited the spot (Covid) but says he has a candidate location in Islamabad.
quote: まず 1 点目は，市から北西 5 マイル（8km 程）の地点の道路の北側にある，高さ 20 フィート（6m 程）の石片に覆われた長いトープである。…捨頭塔は遠くハロー渓谷の北にあるサルダ丘陵でなく，このマールガラ（「首切り」）丘陵の周辺にあってほしいところである。
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Bhallar stūpa, Sarda hill, after Marshall). Naiki accepts Bhallar as fitting distance and bearing from Sirsukh; his move follows only from his relocation of the capital. No remains survive at the proposed site.

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: 拘浪拏塔 (Kunāla stūpa)
asr_identification: the vanished tope at Thupi village, c. 3.5 km SE of the Rawalpindi cantonment, half-way to the Soan river (near the later jail, now Jinnah Park; 'Topi Rakh' park to the S), Rawalpindi, Pakistan
evidence: Against Marshall: the 'Kunāla' stūpa on the Hathial ridge lies c. 3 km SSW of Sirsukh, not SE, and c. 1 km WNW of the far larger Dharmarājikā. Proposed: the second tope of Court's map, between the Rawalpindi cantonment and the Soan, destroyed when its material was taken for the jail; lamps with 'Arian' (probably Kharoṣṭhī) inscriptions from digging near the jail went to the British Museum (Cunningham ASR II, pp. 151–152); a rise survives S of Jinnah Park under the name Topi Rakh. Manikyala, 25 km SE, is too far and on a plain, so not the Kunāla stūpa.
quote: 2 点目は，ラーワルピンディー市中心部にある軍事基地とソーアン（Soan）川のちょうど中間に存在したものである。かつてはトゥピ（Thupi）村の名で知られていたようだが，刑務所を建てる際に部材が遺跡から持ち出され，トープ自体はカニンハム氏の時代にはすでに消滅していた。
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Marshall's stūpa on the Hathial ridge, low). Naiki's bearing objection (SSW of Sirsukh, not SE) is the one the study's note already records (Yamamoto); his candidate is a destroyed mound known from Cunningham, with no excavation. Adds to the open alternatives (with Boyer's Dharmarājikā, which Naiki rejects for this stūpa because no 7th-c. city lies NW of it).

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: 捨身飼虎塔 / マーニキャーラ大塔
asr_identification: not Manikyala (Rawalpindi district, Pakistan)
evidence: Relic deposits from the Manikyala great stūpa (after Errington 2012): the third from the bottom has coins of Kanishka I and Huvishka (late 2nd c.); the fifth from the top, in an iron box, silver coins of Abdallah b. Khazim (685), Tegin of Kabul (c. 720) and Yaśovarman of Kashmir (early 8th c.), so the stūpa was enlarged in the early 8th c. and active in Xuanzang's time. Its surroundings are flat plain, without the mountains and cliffs of the tigress story, so Cunningham's body-offering identification cannot stand (after Kuwayama 1987). Naiki thinks Xuanzang did not pass Manikyala on either journey.
quote: カニンハム氏はマーニキャーラ大塔を中国僧らが記録した捨身飼虎塔と考える説を唱えたが（Cunningham 1871, 102; Cunningham 1872, 154），上述の通り，大塔の周辺は物語に現れる山や崖のある環境ではないため，この比定を受け入れることはできない（桑山 1987, 237）。
note: Agrees with the study (Banj on the Mahaban spur, Stein) against Manikyala; adds the dated relic deposits showing Manikyala active in the 7th–8th c. The argument from terrain is Kuwayama's (1987).

author: Naiki
name_in_asr: シャー・ジー・キー・デリー仏寺址の仏塔
asr_identification: Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, Peshawar (assumed)
evidence: Review of Kuwayama 2022. Summarises his reconstruction of the Shah-ji-ki-Dheri stūpa (a round stūpa damaged before Kanishka's time, encased in a square stūpa with round corner bastions under Kanishka, matching Songyun's 'great towers at the four corners'; the bronze reliquary cast then, pp. 161–162, 176–177) and notes Errington and Falk 2002, who read the 'clay sealing' found with the casket as a Huvishka coin; Naiki supports a Kanishka-period date from the Kharoṣṭhī letter forms. Also mentions Kuwayama's treatment of the Uḍḍiyāna records and the geography of its Buddhist sites, without details. Locates nothing.
note: Dating of the Kanishka stūpa's phases and casket, not its location; no change to 02.04.03 (Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, high).

author: Neelis
name_in_asr: Da-li-luo (Xuanzang); Tuo-li (Faxian)
asr_identification: a valley of an upper Indus tributary between Shatial and Chilas (Darel/Tangir), Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan; exact site unknown
evidence: No archaeological remains of the Maitreya shrine or of the monasteries near it have been found; the upper Indus has abundant Buddhist petroglyphs and Kharoṣṭhī/Brāhmī graffiti (Chilas, Thalpan, Shatial) but no monastic settlement before the Palola Ṣāhis (7th–early 8th c.). Xuanzang probably did not travel the upper Indus himself; his Da-li-luo information is secondhand. Faxian's 'Hanging Passage' is localised in the Indus gorge between Sazin and Besham (Stein 1942; Jettmar 1987).
quote: Archaeological remains of such a shrine have not been found, but Tuo-li may have been located in a valley of an…upper Indus tributary between Shatial and Chilas…Chinese accounts of Faxian and Xuanzang refer to a Buddhist shrine with a colossal wooden image of the future Buddha Maitreya in the upper Indus region. However, its location is unknown
note: Agrees with the study's Darel valley (medium, no site evidence) in placing it on the upper Indus between Shatial and Chilas, but stresses that the shrine is unlocated. Agrees with Mizutani. Supports the study's note that the Life gives Darel as hearsay.

author: Neelis
name_in_asr: Bo-lu-luo (Bolor)
asr_identification: the realm of the Palola Ṣāhis of Gilgit (Little Bolor), Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan; Great Bolor = Baltistan (capital at Katsura near Skardu in 753)
evidence: The Palola Ṣāhis of Gilgit (late 6th–mid 8th c.) are attested as Buddhist patrons in manuscript colophons, rock inscriptions and inscribed bronzes; Xuanzang's Bo-lu-luo is 'this region' of the Palola Ṣāhis, whom he does not mention because his information was secondhand. In the 8th c. Huichao distinguishes Greater Bolor (Tibetan) and Lesser Bolor (Chinese side; presumably the Palola Ṣāhis); in 753 the Chinese took the capital of Baltistan (Great Bolor) at Katsura near Skardu. Bru-za / Little Bo-lu-luo / Bolor is tied to the Burusho ethnonym (Hunza, Nagar, Yasin).
quote: The secondhand nature of this information is probably the reason why Xuanzang does not refer to the Palola Sˢāhi rulers of this region, whose support of Buddhist scholarship in the seventh century was contemporary with Xuanzang’s visit to Swat.
note: Bears on the study's open alternative (Baltistan or Gilgit, the Palola Ṣāhis' kingdom): Neelis takes Xuanzang's Bolor as the Palola Ṣāhi region, i.e. Gilgit, without arguing against Baltistan; Baltistan appears as 'Great Bolor' only from the 720s. Differs from Mizutani (Baltistan). No site evidence; leaves the place open.

author: Neelis
name_in_asr: Varusˢapura (Pa-lu-sha)
asr_identification: Shahr-i Bahlol (Sahri-Bahlol), Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan (after Errington 1993)
evidence: Cites Errington 1993 ('In search of Pa-lu-sha, a city of the central Gandhara plain', BAI 7) for Varuṣapura at Shahr-i Bahlol, an ancient city where extensive Buddhist structures and sculptures have been found since the 19th c., poorly preserved under the modern village; Takht-i Bahi lies a few km N. Neelis gives no argument of his own.
quote: Ancient Varusˢapura (probably localized at Shahr-i Bahlol) was another major ancient city in Gandhāra where extensive Buddhist structural remains and sculptures have been found since the nineteenth century…localizes Varusˢapura (Pa-lu-sha in Chinese accounts of a shrine commemorating the Viśvantara narrative) at Shahr-i Bahlol
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Shahbaz Garhi, after Foucher and Dani; high). Errington 1993 is not in the study's sources; her argument should be read before the Shahbaz Garhi identification is kept at high confidence. Neelis only reports it.

author: Neelis
name_in_asr: shrine of Prince Mahāsattva's bodily sacrifice (Mānikyāla)
asr_identification: not Manikyala, Rawalpindi district, Pakistan; site unknown
evidence: Faxian's tigress site is usually put at Manikyala, whose great stūpa held relic deposits with coins from Huviṣka (2nd c.) to the early 8th c., when it was substantially renovated (Ventura 1830; Errington and Cribb 1992); but Xuanzang's 'great rocky pass' cannot be reconciled with the topography round Manikyala, and he goes on to Uraśā and Kashmir, so his shrine may lie elsewhere in northern Pakistan.
quote: also describes a massive stone stūpa associated with the story of Prince Mahāsattva’s bodily sacrifice but his localization of this narrative at “a great rocky pass” (Li 1996: 99) can not be reconciled with the topography of the area around Mānikyāla.
note: Agrees with the study against Manikyala (the study's choice is Banj on the Mahaban spur, Stein); Neelis names no alternative and calls the geography 'confused'. Mizutani agrees with Banj.

author: Olivieri
name_in_asr: (no name; the area between Manglawar and Mingora)
asr_identification: the left bank of the Swat between Manglawar and Mingora as the core of late (7th–8th c.) Buddhist Swat; no capital named
evidence: Survey of c. 200 late Buddhist rock sculptures (7th–8th c.; Filigenzi 2015): the highest concentration lies on the left bank of the Swat, especially in the left tributary valleys, between Manglawar and Mingora; near Barikot only 3 of 75 Buddhist foundations have them; the lower city of Barikot was abandoned in the 4th c. Around Mingora late Buddhist communities kept wide control of their territory; near Barikot only the valley floor and main roads.
quote: the highest concentration of Late Historic Buddhist rock sculptures was found along the left bank of the river Swat, especially in the left tributary valleys, between Manglawar and Mingora…While in the area surrounding the present city of Mingora late Buddhist communities maintained a wide control of their territory
note: Does not decide between Mingora (study, Mizutani) and Manglawar: the distribution puts the 7th–8th-c. Buddhist centre in the stretch containing both. Consistent with either; the question stays open.

author: Olivieri
name_in_asr: mount Ilam (Hilo)
asr_identification: Mount Ilam (Ram-takht, Jogiano-sar), above Barikot, Swat, Pakistan
evidence: The mountain keeps the Tibetan toponym Hilo (Olivieri 1996, p. 69 n. 33); its Pashto name Jogiano-sar, 'yogins' peak', goes with a folk tale of a Buddhist master and his pupil who died trying to fly from the top.
quote: The major mountain of the Barikot area, the mount Ilam (c. 3,000 ft asl; see Figure 2), known as the Ram-thakht or the “Throne of Rama” of the Hindu tradition, still preserves the Tibetan toponym Hilo
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Mount Ilam); adds name evidence (Tibetan Hilo, cf. Xuanzang's 醯羅 *hila) and a Buddhist folk memory. A name, not a monument.

author: Olivieri
name_in_asr: Swat
asr_identification: Swat valley (context only)
evidence: Barikot stratigraphy and Swat-wide evidence: a gap c. 500–700 (Macrophase 7) with building crisis and abandonment of monasteries; agrarian collapse from the mid-6th c., still visible in the first half of the 7th, possibly from the Late Antique Little Ice Age (536–660); the Śāhi deva temple on the Barikot acropolis built c. 700 (radiocarbon) over demolished Buddhist structures; Barikot named Vajirasthāna in a Śāradā inscription of Jayapāladeva.
quote: Suddenly, from the mid-6th century, agrarian production and Buddhist centers enter a crisis period, whose effects were still visible in the first half of the 7th century.
note: Context for Xuanzang's ruined monasteries in Uḍḍiyāna; locates no Xiyu ji place and says nothing on the capital (Mingora vs Manglawar).

author: Sadakata
name_in_asr: Sirkap, Sirsukh, Taxila
asr_identification: (etymologies only)
evidence: Etymological note: Sirsukh from Cukhsa of the Patika plate (Greek-style c > s), 'Sir' from Skt. śrī, 'kap' from *Kaspi- (Kapiśī, Kadphises, 罽賓); 循鮮 of the Hanshu tentatively = Cukhsa (Sirsukh); Cunningham's Sirkap/Sirsukh ogre legends. Takes Faxian's and Xuanzang's 'cut-head' explanation of Taxila as a Buddhist gloss. No location of a Xiyu ji place.
note: No bearing on the study's identifications of 03.03.* (biblio summary expected Kunāla/Candraprabha place names; the article does not treat them).

author: Tsuchiya
name_in_asr: Darel; Gakuch (Punial)
asr_identification: routes between Darel and Gakuch/Gilgit (context only)
evidence: 1991 survey of petroglyph sites (Thalpan III, Chilas I–II, Partab, Alam Bridge, Danyor, Upper Gakuch) and of Bubur. At Upper Gakuch (Punial, 80 km W of Gilgit) the high plateau connects with valleys leading to Darel; villagers said people from Darel still come on foot to buy wheat (one way only, for tribal reasons). Partab, 5 km S of the Indus–Gilgit confluence, lies at the junction of the routes to Kashmir, Baltistan, Gilgit and Chilas/Darel; many of its petroglyphs were destroyed by blasting for the Karakoram Highway. Xuanzang, Faxian and the Maitreya image are not discussed.
quote: This plateau is also connected with the valleys which eventually reach Darel. A villager of Gakuch pointed out that people from Darel often visit this village to purchase wheat and other necessary household supplies.
note: Context for the Darel (03.01.16) and Bolor (03.02) frame: shows a living route from Darel to the Gilgit river, relevant to the study's Gilgit alternative for Bolor, but locates no Xiyu ji place. Agrees with the study (no change).

author: Verardi
name_in_asr: large, miraculous image of the goddess hewn in the rock; temple of Maheśvara
asr_identification: Kashmir Smast cave (Acimā/Gaurī) with the Vardhamāneśvara (Maheśvara) temple and maṭha, Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
evidence: At Kashmir Smast M. Nasim Khan's excavations (preliminary report 2001; Khan 2003, 2009) found a goddess cult (Acimā/Gaurī) and a Śaiva (Pāśupata) temple with attached maṭha, restituted as a Maheśvara temple of the 5th c.(?); this matches Xuanzang's rock-cut goddess worshipped from all India with a Maheśvara temple of ash-smearing heretics nearby. Verardi offers it as the 'spontaneous' identification and does not test distance or bearing.
quote: It would be spontaneous to identify the goddess with the Acimā/Gaurī of Kashmir Smast:32 in fact, a temple of Maheśvara rose near her miraculous image, clearly a Pāśupata temple, to which came ‘the heretics who cover[ed] themselves with ashes […] to offer sacrifice’.33 It might be identified with the Vardhamāneśvara temple, with attached maṭha, at Kashmir
note: Differs from the study and Mizutani (Karamar hill, by Cunningham's bearing; medium, no shrine found). Kashmir Smast has an excavated Śaiva temple and goddess cult, i.e. a matching monument, which Karamar lacks; but the text's 50 li NE of Varuṣapura is not checked here, and the study puts Kashmir Smast forward for Daṇḍaloka (02.04.15). Record as an alternative to test against the Kashmir Smast reports (Nasim Khan, Falk) in this group.

author: Wong
name_in_asr: Darel
asr_identification: Darel, upper Indus (assumed)
evidence: Survey of colossal Buddhas; opens with the Darel Maitreya after Faxian and Miyaji 1988. No new evidence; she calls the image sandalwood and says Xuanzang reported seeing it, both against the texts (Faxian and Xuanzang say wood; Xuanzang probably reports by hearsay).
quote: Before the Yungang or Bamiyan Buddhas were carved, a colossal image of Maitreya Buddha in sandalwood at Darel had long been known to Buddhist pilgrim-monks.
note: Assumes Darel (study, Mizutani); adds nothing to the location.
